title: The Why
summary: Taoists have The Way, Relazation has the why
body_html:
Slow down. Be quiet. That gnawing in your chest, that crushing pressure making it hard to breathe, that’s you. You’re letting that happen. Unless you’re having a heart attack, and then you really need to seek medical attention. But if you aren’t, then it’s probably stress. Anxiety. Your real arch-nemesis. It’s the most powerful, made up, fictional, yet real, monster we have to fight on a day to day basis. But what would you say if I told you that you have the power over it? You have the kryptonite to put it aside and give you the freedom to live your life the way you want?

How do I know? What makes me the expert? I’m no expert. Never said I was. But I’ve lived a lot of life, seen a lot of things, and battled that monster myself. I fight it on a daily basis. By the way, I don’t like the term “fight” because that is what feeds the monster. Fighting is just a metaphor. And it’s actually a dishonest one because the only real way to fight the monster is to ignore it. To just let it have its fun, knowing that when you release your grip on it, your chokehold, your deathgrip, it begins losing its power. Funny, right? The more you fight it the stronger it gets, the more you just let it be, the weaker it gets.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. Why should you listen to me? Who am I? What’s my story? I’m just a guy, when it comes down to it. An old guy. Who was I? At one time, I was in the Navy. In the Nuclear Power Program. I learned not only how to be a military person, I learned how to run a nuclear power plant. Yeah, that still scares me. I actually stood a watch station called Load Dispatcher. If you were in the Navy, that might mean something to you. I can tell by the really impressed look on your face that you weren’t in the Navy and have no idea what I’m talking about. Load Dispatcher is the most senior enlisted watch station on the ship. Let me take it back a step. What’s a “watch station”? Think about Fast Food. The guy standing at the fry station? Yeah, that’s a watch station. Or the lady at the register? Yep. A watch station is a job that you work for a few hours at a time. The Load Dispatcher is the person who directs the entire electric plant for an aircraft carrier. Talk about pressure. Hey, we’re going to be operating really close to an enemy country and we’re going to turn off all the power and see how quickly you can get it going again! Fun, right?

So that started me off on a path where stress, anxiety and pressure were pretty much things I lived with on a daily basis. But it also taught me about integrity, about attention to detail, and about learning and following procedure. We had to know every step required to do anything with the electric plant, even when a casualty (a bad thing, like a power outage) occurred. We had to know, by heart, by memory, every step we had to perform to make sure the casualty didn’t get worse. And once we got things to a safe spot, we would have to stop, pull out the manual, verify that we took all the appropriate actions, and then follow the procedure from there to get things back to normal operating order. So I learned about control. About always being in control, and to a psychotically detailed level. Which drove me to my interest in Eastern philosophy.

In high school, I had a teacher who talked about transcendental meditation. He got a lot of resistance from the deeply religious kids in my class, and he defended his position by saying that a forest was actually closer to God than a church because God made the forest, man made the church. So to commune with the higher power, whichever you believe in, being out in the woods was the way to go for the direct line. After years of intense control, and after years of always remembering this somewhere in the back of my consciousness, and minutes after picking up a book on world religions, I found Taoism and Buddhism.

Something about them, specifically the philosophical sides, resonated with me. It brought me a sense of peace, a sense of yeah, this is it. This fits my understanding of the world better than what I’ve seen so far. The religious side seemed a little out there, and to be frank, it’s not really necessary. None of what I’ve learned or found requires or contradicts religion. So that’s nice.

So I spent a few years reading about Taoism, and Zen Buddhism, and how to meditate (which is really as easy as just sitting down and not thinking about anything. Really, just breath and let your mind go blank. Think of ripples on a pond after you threw a rock in, and after a time, the ripples get smaller and less frequent until the surface of the water is like glass again. That’s where you’re going to find yourself). I read Laozi, Chuangzi, and Chinese poetry. I learned about sand gardens, and Tai Chi, and Chai Tea. That’s Indian, by the way, but the pun is good all the same.

I had no idea that I was setting myself up with a psychological life jacket.

A number of years later, with my wife, and my son, and my daughter, we went through a family catastrophe. I can’t really describe it in a good way, a way to let you know just how awful it was. And maybe one day I will write that story. For now, just know it was bad, and it was about the most stressful thing you can endure. It’s about the most a marriage can endure. In fact, it’s one of those make or break events. We fought to keep ourselves together. It brought us closer, and even today, while I’m writing this and she’s out of state with our daughter, who just gave birth to her second son, I’m having trouble getting through the day because she became that important to me.

I think all my studying in those Eastern philosophies are the reason we’re together, we’re still sane-ish.

And now, I’m here writing. Why am I writing? I could’ve easily just kept on living quietly, but no, I’m writing this. Why? That’s the question I’m grappling with right now. I guess I feel like it’s time for me to take what I’ve learned, what I’m learning, and pass it on. To try and share my knowledge and experience with those who need it.

Years ago, before the pandemic, I started a YouTube channel for relaxation videos. The name Relazation showed itself to me, and that’s the name I gave the channel. It has exactly one video. You can still look it up. The name found me before I even know what it was meant for. Relaxation is a mashup of relaxation and realization. Because you have to relax to realize. That’s what came to me back then. Now, I have the new thought, Slow Down. Be Quiet. And that meshes with the relax and realize. Because until you slow down and relax, you can’t really be quiet, and it’s not until you are quiet that you can realize. Realize what? That’s for you to decide.

I could tell you my name. But honestly, it doesn’t matter. What matters is whether any of this sounds familiar.

This isn’t a self-help guide and I’m no guru. I’m just a person who may be a little further along the same path you’re walking, and I’m leaving a few notes on the roadside to help you along. So if this sounds like something that could help you, or sounds interesting, feel free to follow along. I’ve got a lot more to learn, and more to share.

—R

title: The What
summary: The monster is real. And entirely made up. Both things are true at the same time.
body_html:
It’s 3am. You’re lying in bed, wrapped up like a burrito in your blanket, nice and safe and warm. But your heart is thumping, your breathing is shallow, you’re sweating. What’s going on? Why do I feel like I’m about to pass out? Why do I feel like this? I’m not in danger. There’s nothing here that can hurt me.

Let’s take a step back. What you’re feeling is your body’s attempt to manage modern life using the tools it has that date back thousands of years. Back when your only concerns were finding enough food to eat while not being eaten by a sabertooth tiger. Fight or flight, kill or be killed, was very real back then. Now that your biggest worries are making sure your bills are paid, or maybe having to face down an HR person for saying things that are “looked down upon”, maybe those drastic measures aren’t strictly necessary. But guess what? That’s all of the tools at your disposal.

To make it easier to understand, and to save me some typing, I’m going to refer to the two major actors in your brain as caricatures. If they come off as too childish, just roll with it. I’d rather be too simplistic than too technical.

The first one I like to call Sarge. Sarge represents your amygdala. That’s the part of your brain responsible for detecting threats and sounding the alarm. Sarge has been around, in one form or another, since the first animal brain. He is fast, loyal, and absolutely convinced that the slightly passive-aggressive email from your boss is the same level of emergency as a predator in the dark. He doesn’t distinguish. That’s not his job. His job is to keep you alive, and he takes it very seriously.

The second is The Professor. He represents your prefrontal cortex, the rational, thinking, “let’s just take a moment here” part of your brain. The Professor is measured. Considered. Patient.

Now here’s the problem. When Sarge fires, The Professor goes *partially offline*. Not as a metaphor. Physiologically. Your body is wired so that in an emergency, you don’t write a pros-and-cons list. You run. Or fight. The thinking brain steps aside so the reacting brain can do its thing.

This works great against actual predators. Not so great against HR.

When Sarge yells, your body jumps. Heart rate goes up. Blood pressure goes up. Cortisol goes up. And digestion stops. Your body decides that hot dog you just ate isn’t a priority. I know, right? With chili, onions and mustard. What does the body know? Anyway, The Professor, like we said, goes partially offline.

All of this is a great design for a short-term emergency. Run, fight, survive, recover. The whole system is built to sprint, not jog.

Here’s the problem. Sarge was never designed for modern life.

The threats we face today don’t resolve in five minutes. The passive-aggressive email doesn’t go away when you run from it. The unpaid bill is still there in the morning. The difficult conversation keeps getting postponed. And every time Sarge reads these situations as emergencies, which he does, because that’s all he knows how to do, your body pays for it.

Chronic stress, which is just Sarge refusing to stand down, comes at a cost. Elevated cortisol over time damages the hippocampus, the part of the brain responsible for memory and context. It weakens The Professor’s ability to regulate Sarge. It drives chronic inflammation, which is linked to cardiovascular disease and a measurably shorter life expectancy, and I don’t mean that loosely. That’s an actual medical finding.

And that’s before we get to the psychological toll. You can’t sleep, your relationships are strained, and you just become numb to it, which makes it even worse, because now you’re not doing anything to course correct.

Here’s the part that took me the longest to figure out. The monster is real. I mean, the heart pounding, the feeling of impending doom, the sleepless nights. But then again, it’s not real. Just the results, or the reaction you experience. That’s real.

But the threat? The thing that set Sarge off?

Not real. At least, not real in the sense that you’re going to be eaten by a sabertooth tiger anytime soon.

That’s the difference between fear and anxiety. The sabertooth tiger about to eat you, that’s fear. The letter you got that tells you to report to HR tomorrow morning, that’s anxiety. It’s like fear without the object to be afraid of. You might get yelled at, but you aren’t going to be digested.

So the cruel part is that your body doesn’t really differentiate between something you need to fear and something that just gives you anxiety. Sarge thinks they’re the same, so he ramps up your body to DEFCON 1.

The monster is real. And entirely made up. Both things are true at the same time.

Okay, great, so now what? Well, there is something you can do. It’s about training your brain. You can rewire, relearn. You can change your brain so that The Professor is stronger and remains in charge longer, especially when it can be. And Sarge learns to relax, take a chill pill and see if it’s really necessary to pull the pin on the grenade. There’s a tool you can use, and next time, we’re going to talk about the people who figured it out a long time ago. Before we even had the science to explain why it works.

—

R

title: The Way
summary: How Stoics, Taoists, and neuroscientists all found the same switch.
body_html:
Last time, we talked about your brain and I tried to make it a more simplified, easier to visualize and understand version by introducing the Sarge (your amygdala) and The Professor (your prefrontal cortex). I don’t want to bore you with a bunch of scientific things, but it’s important to the discussion and going forward to understand a little of the mechanics. If you missed that article, feel free to stop right now, go back and read it. Or, I can give you the quick and dirty version here.

Two parts of your brain, The Professor and the Sarge, handle most of your reactions. In normal, calm, rational situations, The Professor runs things. But when the SHTF, as they say, the Sarge takes charge. He’s just like his name, aggressive, decisive and defensive, and he takes his job of protecting you very seriously. Too seriously sometimes, especially when your biggest danger is a mysterious email from your boss, not a rabid sabertooth tiger. But since the Sarge was created many thousands of years ago, way before computers and the internet, he’s no good at knowing the difference. So he charges in headfirst and boom. Anxiety.

So, we left off knowing there was a way to sort of manage it. In today’s modern world, when the brain gets going like it does, it triggers a lot of physiological responses. Most are out of your control. But you have one that is in your control. And it’s like the Stoics say, don’t worry about what you CAN’T control, focus on what you CAN control. You CAN control your breathing. You CAN’T control your heartrate, or blood pressure, cortisol levels or sweating. Breathing is the key. It’s the lever you can pull to get control back to The Professor and get the Sarge to stand down.

Your breath. The key.

—

I know, you’re like, “what’s a Stoic”? Or maybe you already know. Good for you! That puts you ahead. But in case you don’t know, the Stoics, people like Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus and others, realized that there are things in your control, and things that aren’t. And the path to a happy life (yes, yes, a happy wife is the usual answer), is to understand that and determine which is which. And spend your energy where it’s most effective, not where it’s wasted.

So now, when the Sarge fires up, he raises your heart rate, cortisol level, adrenaline, blood pressure. He’s getting you ready to fight. Or run. And all those things are in his control. But not yours. So a Stoic would look at those things and say, let it go. Don’t fight it. Don’t add to it. You can’t stop it or reverse it. But, the breath is something that’s kinda weird. If you don’t think about it, it happens, and the Sarge controls it. Increasing your oxygen levels, getting your muscles prepared to move. But if you want, you can hold your breath. Or speed it up. Just by thinking it. You have total control when you choose to take that control. Oooo, how very Stoic of you. Epictetus didn’t know what the vagus nerve was, but he knew where you should put your attention.

So what happens when you control your breath, and what exactly should you do? You should slow your exhale down. So you don’t even need to change ALL of your breathing, just the out part. The Letting Go part.

So you have this nerve, the vagus nerve. It’s a long, wandering nerve that connects your brain to most of your major organs. And it has two modes of operation. When Sarge is in charge, the sympathetic branch takes over. Your heart rate goes up, your body goes on high alert, and boom, you’re ready to go. When you extend your exhale longer than your inhale, you switch on the parasympathetic branch. Your body wants to rest and digest. That’s your body’s signal that the fire is out, the war is over, time for some R&R.

So that’s it. The exhale. A longer exhale than inhale tells your body that “we’re safe”. You’ve seen it all the time, when someone gets done with something strenuous, or runs into the cave at the nick of time to avoid the hungry Bengal tiger, they always “whew!” it out. That’s a long exhale signaling that we made it, we’re ready for some food and sleep. And that’s when the Sarge chills and The Professor gets back into the driver’s seat.

So, in the real world, how do I do this? Easy. Breathe in for 2 to 4 seconds, then breathe out for longer, like 6 to 8 seconds. Done. Do that for two to three minutes. You don’t need to be sitting cross-legged. You don’t need to chant or say “Ommmmm”. You just breathe out longer than you breathe in.

This isn’t some metaphysical ritual. It’s not archaic or esoteric or arcane. It’s practical. It’s physiological. It’s a physical nerve that tells your body to calm down.

—

What’s really cool about this is that Taoist breath practices go back thousands of years. They have this thing called Wu Wei, which is working with nature instead of against it, yielding instead of forcing. It shows up in breathing the same way it shows up in Taoism. Don’t fight the body, move with it. Find the flow and use it.

Zen Buddhist monks were basing their entire lives around breath awareness centuries before anyone had even heard of the vagus nerve. They didn’t do it because science showed WHY it worked, they did it because it worked. They found the lever, through practice, and built traditions around it.

The Stoics came at it from a different angle. Through attention and deliberate pause, rather than formal breath practice, they landed in the same place. Marcus Aurelius wrote daily. Epictetus taught his students to create a gap between things that happen and their reaction to it. That gap is what the monks were working on. They just used a different architecture.

Crazy, right? All these practices and traditions separated by geography and time and yet they all found the same lever. That’s not a coincidence.

—

In the early 2000s, Sara Lazar at Harvard started scanning the brains of long-term meditators. She found that regular practice produces measurable structural changes in the brain. Thicker Professor and a stronger connection between The Professor and the Sarge. The Professor literally gets bigger and the phoneline between him and the Sarge gets stronger. Better reception. Can you hear me now?

Richard Davidson at the U of Wisconsin found similar results. Sarge still fires in long-term meditators, but there’s a pause, a gap if you will, between stimulus and response. Hmmm. Viktor Frankl, writing from a Nazi concentration camp in WWII, described that pause as the space where human freedom lives. Years later, neuroscientists could show it on an fMRI. Mind. Blown.

*** Science Alert ***

The phoneline between The Professor and the Sarge is called the uncinate fasciculus. And it gets stronger with practice. Use it and it grows. And The Professor gets LOUDER and the pause gets longer.

This is why breathing matters. You’re not just calming down now, you’re improving that phoneline for the future. You’re installing fiber optics!

Now that we’ve made it this far, I want to introduce you to my last character. I promise. He doesn’t have his own essay yet, but he earns a mention here because this is where he lives.

Sarge fires, The Professor analyzes, but this guy is built through practice. With time and repetition. He’s not reactive like the Sarge, and he’s not purely intellectual like The Professor. He’s practiced, steady. He’s the kind of person who’s been through enough that they don’t need to perform calm. They just are.

I call him The Sage.

The Sage isn’t a brain region. He’s what The Professor becomes when he’s been trained long enough, the version of you that doesn’t have to think about not panicking, because it’s already been built in. He represents everything we’ve pulled from Taoism, Zen Buddhism, Stoicism, and neuroscience, wrapped into something easier to visualize than, say, the uncinate fasciculus. And I won’t try typing that again, I won’t ask you to remember it, say it, read it, or even think about it again. Well, maybe not. We’ll see. But The Sage is a nicer package.

—

So none of this is a quick fix. If it was, I would’ve been fixed years ago. The Taoists knew it, the Buddhists knew it, the Stoics knew it. Neuroscience confirms it. So what you’re building is a practice. Consistency matters more than intensity. A few minutes a day, regularly, does more than an hour once a week. The brain changes slowly, like most real change.

But you don’t have to start with ten minutes. You can start tonight. You could start right now!

2 to 4 counts in. 6 to 8 counts out. Two minutes.

Not a program. Not magic. Just practice.

Slow down. Be quiet. And let it go.

— R

title: The Optometrist Moment
summary: I saw the light. Or, rather, I saw the ocular migraines.
body_html:
I’m sitting at my desk, trying to think of ideas for articles, and great anecdotes to share, when I felt a dimness growing in my vision. I couldn’t even really describe what it felt like, other than a general dimming of my vision. I quickly pulled out my handy database of ophthalmic information, Google, and looked up my symptoms. “Dimming of vision”. Whoa. Don’t ever do that without having an Optometrist standing beside you. Or maybe a bottle of tequila. With a bit of additional anxiety (breath? exhale? who’s got time for that?), I calmly told my hypochondriac wife about it. She did the freaking out for me and called my friendly neighborhood Optometrist.

Before I move on in the story, let me tell you a little I haven’t told you, yet. About a year ago, I went Keto. I cut out sugar totally and it had an effect. I got some major floaters, some ocular migraines (if you’ve never had those, look it up before you do to save yourself a scare.), and general eye unease. I consulted my handy database of ophthalmic information, Google, and looked up my symptoms. Yes, I should’ve learned my lesson this time from that time! It told me about Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Detachment, and a bunch of other things that sounded like pretty terrifying physiological issues. When I went to see my Optometrist and told him about the disastrous state my eyes were in, and explained about the Keto, and going cold turkey on the sugars, and decided I needed to start learning braille, he just kinda looked at me and told me to relax. We went through the checkup and he told me everything was fine, I just had some new floaters and ocular migraines and new floaters were fairly common with big changes to the diet, or stress, or just living for more than a few minutes. He is also a big time nutrition and health guy, so we ended up talking about how amazing it felt being on Keto for close to an hour.

So when my wife relaxed enough to ask me which eye surgeon I wanted to see, I told her that if anyone knew what it was, or how to fix it, or where I could learn Braille, it was my Optometrist.

We got to the appointment, and my optometrist looked in my eyes for a while. He turned the blinding lights off and sat back.

“Stress,” he said.

Then he asked me why I was smiling like the cat with the canary, or the kid in the candy store, or the writer who just found a topic.

Hearing my eye doctor tell me that stress was the most likely cause of my eye issue really made me happy.

“Now I know what my next article is going to be about!”, I told him.

“What is it going to be about?”, he asked.

“This, I said.”

“What? This what?”

“This, this!”. And then I explained to him about Relazation. And you know how something surprises you without being particularly surprising? He did that to me by explaining to me about the prefrontal cortex and the amygdala and the impact it has on vision and vertigo. Which is what I was feeling, I just didn’t know I knew the word for it. And so I was like, “oh, so Sarge is responsible?” and he was like “who?” and then I told him about my articles and we had a laugh and…well, I get carried away.

---

If you’ve been following along, you know the Sarge. He’s the amygdala (in my cartoon world), and is a part of the brain deep in your limbic system, ancient and fast and completely uninterested in nuance. His job is to fire the alarm. He doesn’t ask whether the threat is real. He doesn’t distinguish between a tiger and a passive-aggressive email from someone you work with. When the Sarge has been running the alarm for a long time, even at a low, just above background noise level, cortisol builds up. And cortisol effects you all over. It drives vasoconstriction. Blood vessels narrow. The optic nerve and the retina are sensitive to changes in blood flow. That is my dimming.

Cortisol also disrupts serotonin, which lowers the threshold for cortical spreading depression, the actual clinical name for what happens during an ocular migraine. A wave of electrical silence across the visual cortex. That is why the light does strange things.

And stress hormones hit the vestibular system directly. Cortisol receptors live in the inner ear. If the floor has ever tilted on you during a high-stress period, that’s why. The Sarge was on fire and vertigo was my result.

---

My optometrist wasn’t telling me I was broken, he was telling me my body had been generating noise for a while, and the volume finally got high enough to see. Or not see, in this particular case. This is what living with anxiety actually looks like sometimes. Not a panic attack. Not a breakdown in the middle of a meeting. Just a Monday afternoon when you go to the Optometrist for a major medical emergency and find out your nervous system has been trying to get your attention for weeks.

The question isn’t how to stop the Sarge from doing this. He is going to do it. That’s his job. The question is whether you start reading the signs earlier. The ones that arrive before the ocular emergencies do.

The tight jaw you stopped noticing because it’s always there. The shallow chest breathing you’ve been doing since last week. The tension that has been living between your shoulder blades since that talk with your boss. The body has been sending smoke signals. The vertigo is just what happens when you stop checking the skies for long enough.

Living with anxiety means getting better at reading the early dispatches. Not eliminating the Sarge. Not forcing yourself into calm. Just catching it sooner, when the cost of not hearing it is still small. Lao Tzu, author of the Tao Te Ching, said it best when he said to take care of the big things when they’re little. It’s much easier to pull up an acorn than a giant oak.

> “Confront the difficult while it is still easy;\

> accomplish the great task by a series of small acts.”

Here’s the good news: the same mechanism that helps the vagus nerve helps with vasoconstriction. The slow exhale directly counters cortisol’s effects. Longer on the way out than on the way in. The parasympathetic system engages, cortisol eases, blood flow normalizes.

But the bigger practice is earlier than the exhale. Before the vertigo. Before the dimness. A body scan isn’t meditation for the seriously committed, it’s just asking: what do I sense right now? What has been on overload? Where am I holding something I didn’t even notice I was holding?

It just takes sixty seconds.

> Start at the top of your head and move down slowly. Notice sensation without trying to change anything.

> Scalp and forehead: any tightness? Jaw clenched?

> Shoulders: where are they? Usually higher than you think.

> Chest: shallow or full?

> Belly: held in or soft?

> Hands: gripping something?

> Feet: can you feel the floor?

The Taoists have been doing this for over 2,000 years. Be still, get quiet, listen to your body before it starts yelling. And they didn’t even need an optometrist to suggest it.

Unlike me, I guess. Still learning. Am I getting better? I don’t know. I hope so.

Slow down. Be quiet.

— R

title: I Learned This the Same Time You Did
summary: On using an old tool for a very modern problem
body_html:
Once again, I’m sitting at my desk. Yes, I know, it’s getting old, but soon, that will be a thing of the past. My new desk is a standing desk, so in the future, I’ll start every article with “Once again, I’m standing at my desk”. Fine, that was a joke, but since I try to make all of my articles sound more conversational, I just naturally start with my current situation, which, oddly enough when writing, is sitting, or standing, at my desk.

A quick aside on the name “article”. I, behind the scenes, call these essays. But for me, and probably you, *essay* carries a connotation of something forced upon you. Something required. Something that has to fit within certain rules. I wanted what I write to be a little *freer*, a little more voluntarily taken on. After some time, and a few well-timed YouTube algorithmic synchronicities, I saw a video, or two, raving about the craft of essay writing. Originally, Montaigne, the inventor of the essay, used them as a way to learn new things. In order to write an essay, you have to think. You have take new ideas, or new information, and incorporate them into your existing knowledge base. Like chewing a salad. The lettuce and the tomatoes all get mushed and mixed around, you swallow them, and after a while... Well, maybe this isn’t the best way to describe what I’m writing. Essay is what I call them. And they do for me exactly what they were designed to do. They teach me, or rather, provide the vehicle for my learning.

When you write an essay, you start with a topic, or idea, that you either believe or don’t believe. Then you start your research to prove, or disprove, that idea. And there’s a good chance you’ll come up with contrasting information with both pros and cons to the idea you’re working on. And that’s good. That exercises you beliefs and strengthens your critical thinking. And that helps you to absorb the topic deeper into your mind. You digest it rather than just pass it through the ear canal between the left ear and the right ear. It has time to ferment in the gray matter.

And when I started all of this, I knew so, so little. I knew some about the brain and how anxiety works. But I didn’t know about the exhale. I learned that in *The What*. And I developed that knowledge in *The Way*. I used the power of essay to learn new things that challenged and supplemented what I knew, or thought I knew. And you read those alongside my writing them. So we kinda learned it together. Maybe just off by a few days, but still, that’s pretty wild. Knowledge that *humankind* has known for centuries and now it’s ours! Mwah-ha-ha-ha! Feel the power!

---

When I started all of this, I knew exactly where it would go. I would share a few thoughts on the brain and then spend the next few essays telling you about Taoism and Zen Buddhism and then… Well, I’m sure more ideas would come to me. And that all went out the window pretty quickly when I started to learn things. And something magic happened. My topic list started growing. And growing so fast, I’m not even sure I’m going to be able to write all of them as essays. Or at least individual essays. I may have to combine some. Like this one. This was supposed to be about what I learned about the exhale, and I included what I learned about essays. I have so many ideas to share, I’ve decided some of them will probably be better as Substack notes. Or Tweets. Or Instagram posts. Some might be all of the above. It’s exciting to think I’ve got enough fodder for a whole mountain, when I was worried I would be pumping at a dry well.

So the essays became my discovery log. The topics are things I knew about, or had an interest in, but they were all at the surface level. Like *The Optometrist Moment* from last week. I didn’t know my eyesight issue was stress related until my optometrist told me. In *The Way*, I knew the breath was important, but I didn’t know the mechanism until I wrote the essay. I learned all of this at the same time you did. We’re walking that path, not with me in the lead, leaving notes for you along the way. We’re walking side-by-side and I’m telling you what I’m finding *as I find it*.

Right now, my wife and I are selling our current house and moving into our new house. Well, we’re in the process of both, and the stress levels are off the charts. My eyes aren’t helping as that adds a whole new level of anxiety. Even though I know the cause is stress, and I’m doing my breathing exercises, my *Sarge* is still armed and dangerous.

We were driving yesterday, and my wife, who’s dealing with maybe more stress than me, (I mean, she has to deal with me, on top of all of this other stress) was really feeling it. I told her about the exhale rule, to make the exhale longer than the inhale. She did. She did the breathing, 4 seconds in, 8 seconds out, for about 2 minutes. I watched her. Breathing in, breathing out. And I watched her demeanor change. After those two minutes, she was noticeably calmer. Her voice was more relaxed, her cadence was slower. She had calmed herself down with a technique I had just learned and that I was able to share with her.

I’ve been catching myself when my anxiety starts to peak, and I start my breathing. 4 seconds in, 8 seconds out. And it really does help me get back to me. Exhaling longer than the inhale soothes the vagus nerve and tells your body that everything is okay. That it’s time to rest and digest. And knowing it happens when I do it, and then seeing it happen, in real time, when she did it made me so excited that I was able to learn things that directly helped her. That directly made her life a little better. I mean, that’s the whole point of sharing your life with someone, isn’t it?

Three essays in, and I’ve learned that I’m still able to learn when I let myself be open to it. The potential in that is enormous. Suzuki, the great Zen master, says, “In the beginner’s mind there are many possibilities, but in the expert’s mind there are few”. Taoists say that not-knowing is the condition necessary for learning. A full cup has no room for more tea, but an empty cup has plenty.

So I think *The Way* is more than just a title about the exhale and how it affects your anxiety level. I think this whole thing, Relazation, is *the way*. The way to learn. The way to live with anxiety. The way to move forward. And now I’ve realized the best part, that I’m not ahead of you. I’m right here, with you, as you take every step along your way. So slow down. Be quiet.

—

R

title: The Button I Didn’t Press
summary: On using the double exhale in the field, and finding out it really works. And really works well.
body_html:
Here I am, lying on the weird little shelf, table, ledge wondering how I’d gotten myself into this mess. Probably anxiety again. It’s been a rough few months selling the house, renovating the new house, moving some stuff here and there. All stress, all day. Piling up. And now, even with all I’m learning and testing and practicing I’m here. Staring down the barrel of an angry MRI machine.

How did I get here? I know exactly how, mechanically. The wheelchair rolled me into the room. But how did I end up in the emergency room observation floor with a scheduled MRI on the calendar? I could keep walking backwards, but I won’t. Not yet.

So I find myself on this table, looking up at the ceiling tiles as the MRI techs go through the checklist of “Do you have any piercings? Tattoos? Smuggling silver coins?”. And “Are you claustrophobic?”. After enough “no”s, they’re satisfied and begin to send me into the mouth of the beast. Just before full immersion, they tell me that there will be some really loud noises, and that I’m going to be wearing some noise cancelling headphones playing whatever kind of music I want.

So they put the headphones on my head, and I think the noise cancellation is on the blink because it isn’t super noise cancel-y. And the music sounds like it’s coming from an AM radio in the other room. And that’s fine, I guess, because they then put these wedges, maybe foam, maybe some other non-magnetic material, between the headframe my head is resting in and the headphones. Now they’re nice and tight against my head, providing all the lackluster noise cancellation and AM radio sound they can provide. Then, the techs put this frame over my head and push it down tight. Okay, I’m still okay. I’ve ridden rollercoasters and I’ve ridden motorcycles and, well, I haven’t skydived, but I know people who have. I’m not scared. I’m fine.

They tell me they’re starting. The table starts rumbling. Well, maybe it’s just vibrating. No time to think about that, I see the machine’s gaping jaw start to move over my field of view. I’m in the mouth of the monster. It’s a few mere inches above my face and this weird head frame they put over me. Eh, it’s child’s play. A few more clicks and sounds and then “Oh, my, God” what is that sound? It sounds like a drill. Or a whale. And then there’s Don Henley playing “Boys of Summer” on the AM radio in the other room. And the sound is being swallowed by the MRI monster’s growling and gnashing of teeth. And about now is when I’m really thinking I need out of this thing. My breathing is elevating, I’m starting to feel real panic. And why do I need to scratch my forehead right now?

I remember the techs gave me a rubber bulb attached to a tube that presumably causes a flag to wave, or a whistle to whistle, or some other signal when I squeeze it. And I re-adjust my grip on it as I’m about to squeeze the ever loving sh….Wait. I don’t want to chicken out in the first 30 seconds. Let’s think this through.

But since you’ve been following along, you know the thinking part of my brain is not listening. I’m pure fight-or-flight at this point. I can feel myself circling the panic drain. And then, I breathe in. And then I breathe out for about twice as long. I remind myself to try it, to try the breath thing I’ve been talking about. And I do it. Breathe in and count. One, two, three, four. And out, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. And in, two, three, four. And out. And I can feel myself coming down from the edge. After about ten cycles, I’m okay. I’m in control. I did it.

Now I go back to normal breathing, knowing I’m actually in control, I’m not in danger, I don’t need to scratch my forehead, and I can do this. And then, it’s back. Sudden and more forceful than last time. I’m about to rip the cage off my face and bust my way out of this machine. And I think, in, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. And after a few cycles, I’m back to calm.

Thirty minutes, and many breathing cycles, later they brought me out of the machine. The tech asked how it was. I told them it was the worst experience of my life. Nothing prepared me for the sounds. It wasn’t *just* the sound, or the level, or being strapped down. It was all of those, and Don Henley singing in the other room. It was a real sensory overload and with the background anxiety I’d been carrying around for weeks, it was too much for my rational brain.

---

I’ve been learning these techniques and practicing them a little. I’m working my way up to full-scale meditation. One thing I learned recently is that you can’t get much out of those things if your alarm bells are going off. Trying to sit zazen while you’re facing down a sabertooth tiger just makes your body *more* anxious. Your body starts to think you’re crazy to try to “become one with everyone” while a tiger is trying to make you lunch. So step-by-step, I’m finding my way from the fire into the place where the fire isn’t so hot, doesn’t do so much damage, and is much easier to control.

What I did in the tube, now that I’ve learned more, was really the second thing I would’ve done. And I’m not only learning how to do these things, and when to apply them, but I’m learning what to call them. I call it the *double exhale*, but it’s more of a *doubled* exhale. You’re not breathing out twice, you’re breathing out twice as long as you breathe in. Doubled. And another cool technique I learned is the physiological sigh. Which is actually a double inhale, followed by a long, slow exhale. You inhale as much as you can, then take another quick breath in on top of that. I call it *overbreathing* because you’re breathing more than you can, normally at least. Then you hold it, then release through your mouth, slowly. Let the panic and terror and bad stuff slide out gentle. No need to throw it out into the world, let it escape on its own.

Wait, “stress”, “anxiety”, “terror”, “panic”. Aren’t those all the same thing? That’s what I thought, too. But as I’m learning, I’m wrong on a lot of things, and I’m learning the differences between them all. I’ll tell you all about it when I know more.

For now: four in, eight out, four or five cycles. And now, after experiencing it in a real world situation, I’ve got this. Together, we’re figuring it out.

Slow down. Be quiet.

— R

title: From Stress to Terror
summary: Not every screw needs a hammer. Find the right tool for the mental state.
body_html:
Hey there! I’m glad to see you made it back. How’ve you been? I’ve been doing a lot of thinking and researching since we last spoke. Last week, I told you about my experience in an MRI tube and how I felt. I used words like stress, anxiety, terror, fear, panic. But I used those words in a casual way, interchanging them as if they all meant the same thing. I wasn’t sure if they did, so I did some digging. Turns out I was wrong. At least from a scientific standpoint. Which, it turns out, is kinda important when you’re trying to figure out why you feel a way and how to manage that feeling. Right tool, wrong job. When you have a hammer, everything looks like a screw.

So, what are the words, what do they mean, what do they do and how do I manage them? Stress, anxiety, fear, panic, terror. I’ll break them down one-by-one so we can get on some common terrain.

Stress is your slow clock response. It’s the turtle. Or the follower. It’s the one that acts *after* another of these on the list, as a follow up. Your HPA (Hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal) axis gets the signal that there’s a problem, so it releases cortisol to get your body ready to fight. Or flight. Kill or be killed. Run away or be dinner for some sabertooth tiger.

Cortisol and adrenaline are hormones that raise your heart rate, your blood pressure, your energy level, and get you ready for action. Adrenaline burns off pretty quickly, but cortisol. is. slow. It lasts hours, or days, if you don’t burn it off. (spoiler: exercise) And it lasts long enough that if you have another emergency before you fully rid yourself of the last batch, you’ll get a build up. What is bad about cortisol you say? Cortisol is an anti-inflammatory. Inflammation, it turns out, and you’ll see in later essays, and as a thread throughout almost all of my future writings, is a bad, bad thing. Inflammation causes issues with your heart, your brain, your platelets, your gut. The list is long. It’s bad. And the problem with high cortisol levels for an extended period of time is that your body builds up resistance to cortisol, and it loses its ability to *anti* the inflammation.

How do you deal with this? You need to actually recover. You need time. You need rest. You need Aruba. And exercise, as distasteful as it sounds. Cortisol and adrenaline were put into your system so you could do pushups and run laps, so, the best way to get rid of them is to do pushups and run laps. Or swim. Swimming is good because you don’t look out of place swimming with a Piña Colada like you do running with one. Also, running is hard on your knees. Swimming is a good, gentle, vigorous full body workout. Yoga is good, too.

Anxiety is different. Anxiety is a fear of something that *might* happen. It’s not about a real, actual threat. So you have this thing called *self*. Science calls it your DMN (default mode network). DMN, Daemon? Demon? I cast thee out!

This is your brain’s self-referential system. Your “me”. When “you” have anxiety, your “me” is almost always on, which keeps “your” amygdala active and working towards scenarios and not real threats. Your amygdala, however, doesn’t know the difference between a made up “scenario” and a tiger about to pounce. And unlike a real threat, anxiety has no real physical object and no real timeline. Some *thing,* some *time.*

So how do we deal with this? You have to get your prefrontal cortex back in charge. You have to think, “what am I afraid of”? And get out and touch grass. Wash the dishes. Do something to get your DMN turned off. When you’re thinking about right now, where you are, what’s around you, you can stop worrying about what may never actually come. So the antidote for anxiety is mindfulness. Meditation. Being in the now so you’re not thinking about next week, or next year. “What is actually threatening me right now?”

Anxiety also has a physiological feedback loop that keeps it going. It’s almost like the panic/fear of fear loop, but at a lower level. Anxiety triggers your HPA to release cortisol, which over time leads to cortisol resistance, which allows more inflammation (pro-inflammatory cytokines), which can cross the brain-blood barrier to reduce your serotonin production, which can lead to more anxiety and depression. Whew! That’s a lot of words to say that anxiety leads to more anxiety.

So you have to break the cycle and get your body to get its groove back (reduce cortisol resistance to lower inflammation). And a quick cheat code is a hug. Go hug someone. Hugging someone will trigger the production of oxytocin, which is anti-inflammatory and dampens your HPA axis activity. Petting your dog works, too, so get out there and hug it out, bitches!

So now I know what you’re asking, what triggers your HPA, right? Well, technically all of them. Stress is actually *the* long term HPA response. But the others do at different doses for different lengths of time. So we’ll look at them one at a time.

Fear is what your SAM (sympatho-adrenal-medullary) axis responds to. The sympatho in SAM is for your sympathetic nervous system. More on that later.

Fear is an emotion based on an object. *Something* is about to eat me. This fire is about to burn me. Fear is about things that are going to happen right now if I don’t react. The SAM axis is also, luckily, about the now. It releases adrenaline and noradrenaline that work in seconds and usually clear in minutes to an hour. So you’re pumped up, but it goes away fairly quickly. But, it also triggers your HPA axis, so you will get some long-lasting cortisol, too.

How do you handle fear? Get away from the threat. I mean, literally. Fear is based on *real* threats, so run away, put out the fire, climb a tree. Do what you have to do to survive and your body will handle its own recovery, once you’re safe.

Unless the object is a social or psychological threat. In that case, you’re probably going to have to handle your recovery yourself.

When you experience fear, your amygdala fires off and your prefrontal cortex kinda stops doing its logical thing. You need to turn that around. How? Your vagal brake. My *what*-al brake? Vagal, as in your vagus nerve. The Vagus nerve (we’re going to spend a lot more time on this in the future) is the biggest nerve in your body and it runs from your brain, through your eyes, your carotid, your lungs and ends up in your gut region. And your vagus nerve is *the* trigger from your SAM’s archnemesis, your parasympathetic nervous system. Your PNS (heh, heh) shuts down your sympathetic nervous system. This allows your body to rest, digest, and recover. How do you activate your vagal brake? There are a number of techniques, but you already know the one I’m going to mention, if you’ve been reading along with my other essays. Which I know you have. Ding! Ding! Ding! The double exhale. Breathe in, then breathe out for around twice as long. A slow, mouth exhale. Within a few breathes, your vagus nerve should be actively igniting your PNS.

Now you can name the object of your fear and take its power away from it. You start transferring power back to your prefrontal cortex, which takes control away from your amygdala, and brings balance to the force. Once you’re thinking logically, and you’re not in fear of the object, your body will continue to restore itself from the response. It knows what to do, you just have to give it the chance.

Panic is the next step up from fear. It’s basically a self-amplifying loop. You’re afraid, so your body responds, which increases your heart rate, blood pressure, chest tightness. And now you think you’re having a heart attack. Which leads to more fear, more response, more of all the bad. Which means panic is fear of fear itself. Very Churchill-ish. Actually, it’s the fear of the fear *response*, but my way sounds cooler. Like t-shirt potential cool.

So, we know what it is, how do we deal with it? First, panic only lasts up to about 10 minutes, so if we do nothing, it goes away on its own. Yay! Easy, peasy. So now that you know, remember that if you ever panic. And oddly enough, that’s really the best way to deal with it. Just acknowledge it and know it’s going to go away. If you fight it, that actually makes it worse. It feeds into the secondary fear and increases the response. But it’s still going to go away. So why fight it? Breathe instead. Take a breath, think about the breath you’re taking. The panic will pass. Like last night’s dinner.

I’ve saved the worst for last. Terror is not higher panic. Terror represents the activation of the dorsal vagal branch of the autonomic nervous system. This is distinct from the sympathetic nervous system, the fight-or-flight response.

Here we get into Polyvagal theory (Stephen Porges in the 1990s), which describes the branches of the autonomic nervous system operating in a hierarchy. The autonomic nervous system includes the sympathetic, the parasympathetic, and your gut system. The Ventral vagal is your safe, social, regulated branch. That’s at the top and where you want to be. Your Sympathetic is your fight or flight branch, below that, and where you don’t want to be. And the Dorsal vagal is the reptilian branch for immobilization, conservation and shutdown, at the bottom, where you really, really don’t want to be.

So with terror, you start out in a really intense fight or flight but with no way out. That’s the difference between fear and terror. Fear, you can fight, you can run. Terror, you’re stuck in that proverbial quicksand all the 80s tv sitcoms were always trying to convince us are such common threats. I’ve only been stuck in quicksand once and it wasn’t so bad.

When you can’t fight or flight, or when things are too intense, or you just can’t leave, the system stops escalating. You drop out of sympathetic into dorsal vagal. Your heart rate drops, your metabolism slows. You start to dissociate. You get the famous *thousand yard stare*. You look calm, but your nervous system has basically thrown in the towel.

The trigger is *intensity* and *no exit*.

This can be chronic, too. Low grade. It’s common and usually underrecognized. You have brain fog, emotional numbness. You feel like you’re just going through the motions. You can live in it for months without realizing it’s a nervous system state.

So how do you get back? Gentle physical movement. Warmth. And being around someone whose nervous system is regulated.

You can move back up the ladder, first to the sympathetic branch, and then back up to ventral vagal. When you hit the sympathetic branch, you’re going to experience those heightened heart rates and blood pressures. You’re awakening back into fight-or-flight. It’s temporary, and necessary, so it’s good to have support for it. But it’s just a step to recovery.

Each of these states has a recovery and they’re different.

The double exhale works for fear and panic. It doesn’t reach dorsal vagal shutdown. Each state needs to be handled differently. Knowing which state you’re experiencing will help you reach for the right tool.

The throughline is the breath. Double exhale is great for quickly activating the vagus nerve to counteract fear and panic. Daily practice with the double exhale will build up your brain’s ability to handle stress and anxiety. Breathing is even good for recovering from dorsal vagal when you use it at the right times. Who would’ve thought the most effective and versatile method would be free, easy and readily available in unlimited supply.

So remember, no matter which state you’re in, or how badly you’re dysregulated, you can recover. And it starts with breathing. Like Mr. Miyagi once said, “Don’t forget to breathe.”

Slow down. Be quiet.

— R

Thanks for reading Relazation — Learning to Live with Anxiety! This post is public so feel free to share it.

title: No One Teaches the Return
summary: What military stress training skipped and how veterans can recover without asking for help
body_html:
The day was gray. I mean, mentally, physically, meteorologically. It was gray. Cold and gray, cloudy, windy, and off in the distance, across the gray water slid the gray behemoth making its way out of Hampton Roads, and out of my life, carrying with it just about everything I’d known, almost everyone I’d known, for the past few years. And there I was, standing alone, on the pier, with my freedom, my possibilities and my loneliness. It was my first day of separation from the Navy, and the first day of my ex-ship’s next cruise. All the guys I’d spent the last few years with, my brothers, my family, my identity, sailing off into the gray.

Separation, if you’re not familiar with military life, is a bittersweet moment. You’re now at the whim of your own personal choices. You can sleep in. You can take the day off. You can choose to not go out to see for months at a time. You can make plans for more than a week in the future. I mean, it’s up to you. You can decide that the second weekend of the month, six months from now, that yes, you absolutely can go to the beach. And with that freedom comes the isolation. The loss of that support group. That loss of the only people who really get your sense of humor. Or understand why you feel the way you feel, or why you do the things you do, or why you say the things you say. And it’s a real loss because as a military member, you’re probably not *from here*. You’re probably from wherever you call home. Wherever your family is. Your real, biological family, or whatever passes for it. You’re from Ohio (probably). Or Texas. Or California. You’re not from Virginia, and if you are from Virginia, you’re probably not from Hampton Roads. Norfolk.

So when you get back to where you’re from, all those guys, and gals, won’t be there. And back when I separated, there weren’t the connections like today. So at least those getting out today have that going for them. But distance is time, and time adds to the distance and closeness slips away. And they’re going out tomorrow for a two week cruise, so they won’t be able to talk to you. And they’re still living in the structured, “everything is already planned for you” world, so they won’t know how to help you manage your new life.

So you struggle with a lot of things you didn’t expect to struggle with. And on top of the loss of community, support and mission, you also have a psychological weight to carry. Boot camp did a lot for us. It taught us to become, nearly, completely dependent on our command structure to structure our lives. To tell us when to eat, when to sleep, what to wear, how to fold what we’re going to wear, how to stow what we just folded. We’re told almost everything we need to do. And we’re trained. We’re giving a very special ability that isn’t really even spelled out. We’re given stress inoculation. Whoah, what’s that? Is that what was in those airguns they shot into our arms? No, that was regular inoculations. But the parallel is there. Viral inoculations are a low dose of something potentially very bad given to us in a way that our body builds up the ability to handle it. That’s what those shots did for viruses. Stress inoculation works similarly. We’re giving stressful situations and taught to act under pressure. We need that ability to enter a combat arena and not shut down. To be able to fix that leaking bulkhead. Or get that reactor back online. Or duck down in the foxhole. I guess. That’s more of an Army thing.

Stress Inoculation Training (SIT) was developed as a way to get you prepared to be able to act in a stressful environment. Military gets it. First responders get it. A close analog is called stress resistance, and it’s what comes naturally for people who live in stressful environments. People who grew up with domestic violence, or things we tend to not talk about. But with SIT, you’re taught it in an environment where you know the Navy has your back, when it comes down to it. And the stress ends. With stress resistance, it doesn’t end, you know it’s always there.

SIT comes from a training program Donald Meichenbaum created in 1985. It had three phases. The first phase teaches you what stress is and how it works. Phase two shows you how to come back from the stress. Phase three exposes you to stress gradually so you build up a tolerance. Phase one and three helped us fulfill our role. Phase two wasn’t necessary to the mission, so it was skipped in boot camp.

That’s the return we need physiologically. We need to know how to recover. Here’s something. Only around 12% of veterans get mental health service. Why? Self-reliance. Where did that come from? We were taught that in the service. First responders, you’re not off the hook. 33% of first responders say there’s a stigma attached to getting help and 90% say that stigma is career impacting. So whether it’s from a taught sense of self-reliance or fear of damaging a career, we don’t get help.

So what can we do? I’m looking for ways to help us make ourselves better on our own. Let’s be self-reliant, if that’s who we are, and do it ourselves. Let’s make it our mission to get the skills to recover.

Here’s a couple of quick things I’m trying and I’ve already seen some benefit. Let’s continue getting stress resilient.

First, in the morning, before you get your day going, do some resonance breathing. It’s easy and free and directly raises your HRV (heart rate variability), which is a measure of how resilient to stress you are. So the breathing is simple. Breathe in for 5.5 seconds, then breathe out for 5.5 seconds. Do that for 5 minutes. You should be at a rhythm of around 6 breaths per minute, which synchronizes with your cardiovascular rhythm of around 0.1hz. The Catholic rosary, Hindu pranayama and Zen chanting are all at about the same rhythm. It’s been around for a long time and now science has shown why it works. And you can do it anywhere, with no equipment, and for free.

Second, also in the morning, when you’re at the end of your nice hot shower, turn the water as cold as it gets. And stand there for at least 20 seconds. Your norepinephrine spikes, your brown fat activates, and you’re practicing tolerating acute discomfort. This is training. You’re training your body that it can recover from uncomfortable (stressful) situations. You’re conditioning your nervous system’s recovery response. And after a week or so of doing this, it won’t be so bad and you can stay longer. You want to aim for about 3-4 sessions per week for a total of about 11 minutes. 20 seconds of exposure, then dry off and let your body warm up on its own.

What about the separation? How do you work with that? Community. Find veterans, or first responders, or a knitting circle, or a book club. Find a group of people that can share your interests and show you support. Veterans finding veterans and first responders finding first responders helps on an additional level because you’ve got shared experiences and have that automatic trust built in. So what is it about community that works? Aside from finding people to network with for finding jobs, or learning how to make a dental appointment, you get some physiological benefits. You get co-regulation. When you’re around someone who has a well regulated nervous system, your nervous system will pick up on it and follow their lead. Being around someone with your shared experiences adds the trust multiplier, which lowers your autonomic cost because you don’t have to work as hard to assess safety. Which makes co-regulation even more efficient. That social contact also releases oxytocin, which lowers your cortisol. That lowers your stress load. You know why the military made us march together, eat meals together, suffer together? Yup.

Peer support works. Veteran peer support programs show measurable outcomes. They reduce PTSD symptom severity, improve the likelihood you’re going to get help.

We were trained to operate inside a system and nobody taught us how to recover. The physiological return and the social return. Both are similar shapes. They taught us how to get in, but not how to get out. Stress Inoculation Training skipped phase 2, we didn’t teach our nervous systems how to get back. Practice fills that gap. You can do it yourself, at home, in private, for cheap. Civilian life removed our unit, our structure and our mission. Social organizations can help restore all three.

The return is a skill. At two levels. Physiologically and socially. We weren’t taught how to return, but we can learn it.

— R

title: The Right Tool for the Job
summary: Why meditation doesn't work when you're panicking, and what does
body_html:
There I was, gasping for breath, hands shaking, heart racing, needing a way to calm down, center myself, regain control. I opened my calming app, put in my AirPods and started listening. And within seconds, I was even more anxious. It’s not helping. I’m not getting calmer, I’m getting worse! What’s wrong with me. Am I unable to calm down? What am I doing wrong.

Yeah, that’s a thing a lot of people experience. You’re doing the right thing with the wrong tool. You see, as we discussed, when you’re experiencing a lot of stress, it’s like you’re fighting a fire. It’s here, it’s immediate and you need a fire extinguisher. The calming apps are teaching you a fire prevention system, not a fire extinguishing technique. Mindfulness, meditation, Zazen, body scans. Those are great when you’re not in a crisis. But they’re like trying to install a sprinkler system while your house is burning down. Wrong tool for the job.

So what are we talking about here? The “fire” is anxiety, terror, fear. Things we’ve looked at before. They’re things that cause your body to drop into the fight-or-flight state. When you’re in fight-or-flight, you’re not thinking rationally. Logically. You’re trying to survive. Your sympathetic nervous system (SNS) is running the show. Your heart rate goes up, your blood pressure goes up, your cortisol and adrenaline go up. You’ve heard this, but maybe you didn’t connect the dots. When you’re not thinking logically, you can’t begin to do a technique that requires your prefrontal cortex to participate. You need your parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) to get involved. You need a vagal brake.

Vagal brake? What’s that about? Your vagus nerve is the longest nerve in your body. It runs from your brain, through your eyes, through your neck, through your heart, your lungs and into your intestines. It sends signals to your brain telling it to calm down. You activate your vagus nerve with your fire extinguishers!

What are the fire extinguishers? Well, the quickest to do, easiest to remember and the fastest acting is the physiological sigh. This should be your first choice when you’re under a load of stress. Take a deep inhale through your nose, then another quick inhale on top of that (double inhale), then let it all out very slowly through your mouth. Do this again. By now, you should be about 80% calmer. This action activates your vagus nerve, telling it you’re okay, there’s no need for panic, let’s just calm down and talk about it. Your vagus nerve tells your brain that everything is cool. Your brain tells your body to slow your heart rate, lower your blood pressure, stop producing adrenaline and cortisol. To come back from the edge.

What do you do now that you’ve gotten some control? Now is when I go for the big daddy. The OG. The extended exhale. Breathe in for 2-4 seconds, then exhale for double that. I like to aim for 4 seconds in, 8 seconds out. When you’re panicking, you’re probably not able to take slow breaths like that (this is what the physiological sigh helps with, getting your breathing a little more manageable), so you can take shorter breaths, just make sure the exhale is longer than the inhale.

Now you can add on other techniques, like panoramic vision. Just let your vision go soft and see if you can see things in your peripheral vision. When your sympathetic nervous system is running things, you get tunnel vision because your body becomes focused on the threat. The tiger stalking you, or the ghost coming through the doorway, or your boss walking into your cubicle. Softening your focus tells your vagus nerve, “I’m not tracking a threat, so calm down”.

These are your fire extinguishers. There are more, but these are easy to do, easy to remember, and you can do them without looking like a freak. No one will be counting your breaths and say, “Gee Jim, I see you’re exhaling roughly twice as long as you’re inhaling. Are you mental?”

So when your SNS is on fire, do those. Calm yourself down. Regain control. Come back when you’re more relaxed.

Are you feeling better? Good. Had a nice meal? Slept some? Awesome. So how do we train ourselves to better handle those fires? How do we mitigate their strength? How do we make sure they happen less frequently and that we maintain better control when they happen? That’s where the sprinkler system comes in. Or even something simple, like moving gas soaked rags away from a heat source.

Let’s look at meditation. And mindfulness. And body scans. If you sit for five to ten minutes a day, doing mindfulness practices, you will change your brain. In eight weeks of doing daily meditation practice, your brain will literally re-wire itself. Your white matter will increase, which will give more time for your prefrontal cortex to tell your amygdala to dial it down. Your amygdala will actually shrink! There are studies that show this. Don’t take my word for it.

Your DMN (default mode network), the part of your brain that scientists think acts as your “self”, quiets down. When you’re busy doing things, your DMN is quiet and you don’t think about “you”. When you’re sitting in the waiting room, waiting to be called back to get weighed on the scale, and to see how high your blood pressure is, and the magazines are all women’s magazines from the 90’s, so you start thinking about “did I turn the oven off?” and “did I pay the water bill?” and your anxiety starts climbing because you’re ruminating. Keeping your DMN quiet helps to lower that background stress level that your ruminations keeps trying to turn up.

So how do you meditate? There are a lot of ways, and they all take some degree of learning. But one of the threads running through them is breathing and to stop thinking about yourself. Breathing. Here’s where the extended exhale shows up again. It’s a real two-fer. It’s not just a fire extinguisher! Wait, there’s more! If you practice extended exhale for 3-5 minutes, a few times a day, within a few weeks you will actually lower your blood pressure. There are studies. Amazing, right? And you already know how to do it! 4 seconds in, 8 seconds out. You can do it on the bus, the train, at your desk. Anywhere. Anytime.

What else? Something like Zazen (just sitting) is great for it. Thousands of years of Zen monks can’t be wrong, right? How do you do it? There are a lot of variations, but basically, you sit on the floor, cross legged, and gaze softly at the floor. Set a timer, or use one of the ones I have on my YouTube page, and just sit. Thoughts will arise, just notice them and let them go. Don’t actively try to chase them away, that will lead to more. Your thoughts are going to be like ripples on a pond. At first, there’s a lot of waves, but over time, your mind pond will settle to a glassy surface. Need help? Count your breaths. One, two, three. Count to ten. Once you get to ten, start over with one. Lose count? Start over. Get distracted? Start over.

There are others, and I’ll cover them more explicitly in the future. For now, just know that they are there. And that they take time. These aren’t instant fixes. These take practice and time. Weeks. But they work. The effects are there and you will notice them down the road. You will be more calm, more peaceful and react more thoughtfully.

Still want proof? Okay, your HRV (heart rate variability) is a measure of your body’s ability to handle stress. It’s a measure of your sympathetic nervous system compared to your parasympathetic nervous system. Your Apple Watch already records it in your Health app. Check under the Browse option and you’ll see it under Heart. Other devices will track it for you, too. There are recommended ranges you should be in based on your age, so the older you are, the lower your range, the lower your stress handling capabilities. I think that’s because of the kids. They don’t just give you gray hairs. So, your HRV. Check it now. See what it is and don’t worry about remembering it, Apple Health app will track it for you.

Resonance breathing. This is a fire prevention system and you can do it daily. It’s super easy, especially with a breath prompt that will tell you when to inhale and when to exhale. You want to aim for 5.5 seconds in, 5.5 seconds out. That’s about 6 breaths per minute. Which is resonant with your cardiovascular frequency. Your resting heart rate *should* be around 60 to 70 beats per minute, depending on your fitness level. So your breathing is coherent with your heartbeat. Do resonance breathing (also called Coherent breathing) for five minutes a day and check your HRV. You probably won’t notice anything for a week or two, but it should start going up, indicating your stress tolerance has increased. From breathing. For five minutes a day.

Fire prevention systems take a while to install and train, but they get there. And they minimize your fire possibility and magnitude. Fire extinguishers get the fires knocked down quickly so you can function. Each has a purpose and a time for its use. A lot of people tell you *how* to sit Zazen, or how to do a body scan. But they don’t tell you that you need to be rational to use them. They don’t tell you that you can’t install a sprinkler system if the kitchen is burning, or that removing those gas soaked rags doesn’t work when they’re on fire. I mean, maybe it does, but it’ll probably burn you in the process. It’s better to just spray some CO2 on it and deal with it when it cools off.

They always say that when you only have a hammer, everything looks like a nail. And when you only know how to do a body scan, well, you’re not going to be able to get your nervous system to a place where you can do that body scan. The right tool for the right job. And having the tools is one thing, but knowing why one tool won’t work and why another will is what empowers you to make the right choice in managing your stress.

Slow down. Be quiet.

—R
